doc.title: Onaje Allan Gumbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001

title: Buffalo, the Revelot club, Norman Connors and Phyllis Hyman
summary: Working in a Model Cities program in Buffalo, he meets visiting stars at the Revelot, then arranges for Norman Connors and Phyllis Hyman.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: I had passed through Buffalo but I’d never stayed in Buffalo. So I met some musicians during that time and he called me and said we have a program, we’d like you to teach, it’s a Model Cities program. And it turned out that this program fit the requirements of a CO deferment. Because it had to be a nonprofit organization, more than fifty miles away from your home base. Voila. So I started working right away. I didn’t wait for them to assign © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -9-

me, I just started working. And they wrote the person who was in charge, Sabu signed a form, I had to send away to show what I was making and all that kind of stuff. So about six months later I get reclassified. So I’m relieved of my CO classification, but in other words you’ll never be called. You don’t have to do service anymore and don’t worry about being called. But since I was working up there in Buffalo and getting paid, and going through this whole thing with the music and the culture and everything, I decided to stay. I could have left right then but I decided to stay in Buffalo. And I stayed there almost two years, where I also met my wife. And the benefit of that is that there is a club called the Revelot, and all the cats came through. All the cats came through. Herbie and Ahmad Jamal, Rahsaan Roland Kirk, Freddie Hubbard, Roy Ayers, George Benson, endless stream of musicians, Pharoah Sanders. And again that was where Buffalo was again a definite nourishing environment for me to develop some things I hadn’t done before like my arranging and it afforded me the opportunity of meeting some of these great musicians on a one-on-one basis. Because the thing with the Revelot was that most clubs, if you do a week it’s six days. You start on Tuesday and work through Sunday. Revelot has a very interesting policy. You started on Monday and you’re off on Wednesday. And then you do a matinee on the following Sunday. And at the matinee you can come and sit in with the artists. You can sit in with Herbie Hancock, sit in with Rahsaan Roland Kirk, Freddie Hubbard, whoever. So that was pretty cool. So I had sown the seeds for the future by meeting all these cats that I was able to talk to and get to know what I would be doing in New York. And it was something that was really great. And one of the people again who was a mentor of sorts was Norman Connors. Because he came through with Pharoah, a week right behind Herbie and his group, and commissioned me to do the title track of his second album. Because I just approached him and said I can be the guy you want. Because he was looking for a certain type of arranger who could do strings and do a tune in Brazilian flavor. He just like hit two buttons with that. Because I was doing strings in college and Brazilian music was like my favorite. So from there he listened to, again, my tapes in college, and I got the gig. You know so that was my first major recording situation. And from there I went to work with him, about six months. So I’ve done about maybe five or six albums, and most notably was my arrangement of “Betcha By Golly Wow,” for Phyllis Hyman, which launched her career. And I went on to be her musical director and recorded one more time with her. Well actually we did a whole album at the beginning of her career and then two years later I did one song called “The Answer is You.” And again this whole eclectic thing was happening. I was still going between straight ahead cats and R&B cats and so there is one thing that I really feel is really important in the music is that we get further away from being so concerned about what it is and start being concerned about what it does you see.
